summary: This Standards Track document defines an optional STAMP extension letting a Session-Reflector send response packets whose size or number differs from those the Session-Sender sent, to better mimic application traffic.

plainLanguage.summary: When playing catch, the ball you throw back can be a different size, or you can throw several.

questions: simple two-way active measurement protocol extension
what is the reflected test packet control tlv
what does the c flag mean in stamp
subtitle: An optional STAMP extension that lets a reflector answer with packets of a different size or number than it received.

tldr.problem: Standard STAMP is symmetrical: the Session-Reflector sends back one packet of the same length for each test packet. That cannot imitate application traffic or support rate measurement, where the return path may need more, fewer or different-sized packets.
tldr.mechanism: The Session-Sender adds a Reflected Test Packet Control TLV that asks for a reflected packet length, a number of reflected packets and an interval in nanoseconds between them. Optional Layer 2 and Layer 3 Address Group sub-TLVs limit which reflectors answer.
tldr.outcome: RFC 10052 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2026. Reflectors must enforce rate and volume limits, mark capped replies with a new C flag, and keep the feature disabled by default.

facts.label: Default state
facts.value: Disabled by default on a reflector

today: RFC 10052 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2026. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current definition of this STAMP extension.

sections.title: Why Asymmetrical Reflection
sections.content:
The Simple Two-way Active Measurement Protocol (STAMP, RFC 8762) has a Session-Sender that sends test packets and a Session-Reflector that sends them back. By default the exchange is symmetrical: the reflector sends the same number of packets as the sender, and each has the same length as the packet it answers.

Some scenarios need otherwise. Rate measurements discussed in RFC 7497 benefit from a reflector that answers with packets of a different length, or with packets not sent in direct response to a received one. This document defines an optional extension, building on the TLV structure of RFC 8972, that lets the sender ask for this.

The text uses asymmetrical in two senses: a reflected packet whose size differs from the packet it received, and a reflector that sends a different number of packets in response to a single STAMP-Test packet. It also analyzes the challenges of active measurement in multicast networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the helper at the other end throws back one ball, the same size as yours. This lets you ask for a bigger ball, a smaller ball, or a few balls in a row.

sections.title: The Reflected Test Packet Control TLV
sections.content:
The extension adds one TLV, the Reflected Test Packet Control TLV, and one new STAMP TLV flag. The TLV carries STAMP TLV Flags (one octet), Type (one octet, set to 12), Length (two octets, which MUST NOT be smaller than 12 octets), and then three request fields.

  • Length of the Reflected Packet: two octets, the requested length of a reflected test packet in octets.
  • Number of the Reflected Packets: two octets, how many reflected packets the reflector is asked to send for each received test packet.
  • Interval Between the Reflected Packets: four octets, the gap in nanoseconds between consecutive reflected packets.

An optional Sub-TLVs field follows. The new flag is the one-bit C flag (Conformant Reflected Packet, bit position 3). A Session-Sender MUST zero it on transmission, and the reflector MUST ignore its value on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: The TLV is a short order form. It says how big the returned packets should be, how many, and how long to wait between them.

sections.title: How the Session-Reflector Responds
sections.content:
A Session-Sender MAY include the TLV in a STAMP test packet. If it does, the reflector MUST send a sequence of reflected packets. The length of each is the larger of two values: the length of a base reflector packet (including the STAMP extension TLVs present, but excluding any Extra Padding TLVs), and the requested length rounded up to a four-octet boundary. If that is longer than the length the rules of RFC 8972 would give, the reflector MUST use the Extra Padding TLV to reach it.

The number of packets MUST equal the Number of the Reflected Packets field. When it is greater than 1, consecutive packets MUST be separated by the interval requested. If the number is 0, the reflector MUST NOT send any reflected packets and SHOULD discard the received test packet, although local policy MAY override this.

Two limits protect the network. If the calculated length exceeds the MTU of the interface towards the sender, the reflector MUST set the C flag to 1 and send a single packet whose length equals that MTU. A reflector MUST also enforce limits on data rate (bytes per second) and total data volume of the STAMP payload it generates in response to one test packet. If a request would exceed either limit, it sets the C flag to 1 and sends a single packet of the length calculated above. Otherwise it sets C to 0.

A sender can tell the two C-flag cases apart. A reflected packet shorter than the requested length means the MTU was exceeded. A packet equal to the requested length means the rate or volume limits were hit.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper checks your order. If the box would not fit in the mailbox, or you asked for too many too fast, the helper sends just one box and puts a flag on it to say it could not do what you asked.

sections.title: Choosing Which Reflectors Answer
sections.content:
In a multicast test, one packet can reach many reflectors and trigger a flood of replies. Two optional sub-TLVs let the sender narrow the field. Each reflector applies a mask with a bitwise AND to its own addresses. If the result equals the group value, it keeps processing the packet. If no address matches, it MUST stop processing the packet.

  • The Layer 2 Address Group sub-TLV (Sub-TLV Type 10) carries a mask and a group value of equal length. It can convey EUI-48, EUI-64 and a 16-bit short address. Valid Sub-TLV Length values are 4, 12 and 16, and any other value is a malformed sub-TLV.
  • The Layer 3 Address Group sub-TLV (Sub-TLV Type 11) carries a Prefix Length, a three-octet Reserved field and an IP prefix. The Sub-TLV Length is 8 for IPv4 or 20 for IPv6, and any other value is malformed.

For Layer 3, the reflector builds a mask with the n most-significant bits set to 1, where n is the Prefix Length, and compares the masked address with the IP Prefix. The document also requires a multicast network that estimates rates while in service to use a rate control mechanism that bounds probe generation, and implementations SHOULD let operators configure rate limits and pacing.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine shouting a question in a big hall. These labels say which people should answer, for example only those whose name tag ends in a certain way, so you are not buried in replies.

sections.title: Rate Measurement and Multicast in Practice
sections.content:
For rate measurement, RFC 7497 says a test protocol needs control over packet characteristics such as asymmetric rate and asymmetric packet size. The new TLV supplies the number, size and spacing of the reflected packets. The access-rate metric and method themselves are out of scope. For out-of-service tests an operator may use very high rates or volumes to create congestion at the bottleneck, while for in-service tests the operator may start low and increase gradually.

In a multicast tree the sender is the root and the reflectors are the leaves. A reflector uses the source IP address of the received test packet as the destination of its reply, so a sender may receive many replies. Examples in the text: a Layer 2 mask of 0xF with group 0x1 lets only 1 out of 16 reflectors reply, and a mask of 0xFFFFFF000000 selects a vendor's network interface cards. The Length of the Reflected Packet should be just large enough to carry the timestamps and requested information.

The TLV can be combined with the Return Path TLV of RFC 9503 to send reflections to a collector. A sender MUST NOT combine a Return Path Control Code of No Reply Requested with a non-zero Reflected Test Packet Control TLV. It can also be combined with the Class of Service TLV to check DSCP and ECN consistency in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to test how fast a pipe is, you need to be able to push lots of water through it. And if many helpers might answer at once, you can pick which ones should.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Spoofed test packets carrying this TLV can be used for a denial-of-service attack, because one small packet can trigger many large replies. Implementations MUST use an identity protection mechanism, for example checking the packet source against a list of trusted nodes. They MUST provide administrative control over support for the TLV, with it disabled by default, and SHOULD use STAMP authentication mode or the HMAC TLV.

A reflector that supports the TLV MUST limit the reflection rate and volume. In multicast, the first test packet should use conservative parameters, such as a Number of the Reflected Packets of one, so the sender can count how many replies come back. To resist replay, a reflector SHOULD check that the Sequence Number increases monotonically. If it does not, the reflector MUST answer with a single reflected packet and set the U flag to 1. That may reflect reordering or duplication rather than an attack.

A sender SHOULD NOT send its next test packet with this TLV before the reflector is expected to finish the previous sequence. The text also covers ECN marking during in-service capacity measurements and points to RFC 9097 for security requirements on asymmetric UDP loads.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could trick the helper into throwing a huge pile of balls at someone. So the helper keeps this feature switched off unless an adult turns it on, checks who is asking, and never throws more than a safe amount.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned three kinds of values, all referenced to RFC 10052. In the STAMP TLV Types registry, value 12 is the Reflected Test Packet Control TLV. In the STAMP TLV Flags registry, bit position 3 is the C flag (Conformant). In the STAMP Sub-TLV Types registry, value 10 is the Layer 2 Address Group and 11 is the Layer 3 Address Group, both used with the Reflected Test Packet Control TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of codes got three new entries, so everyone uses the same number for the same thing.
